title: See where an infrastructure failure stops
description: Switch scenarios to trace the active path, identify failed or degraded components, inspect ownership boundaries, and compare the user-visible blast radius.

nodes.label: Customer client
nodes.detail: Starts the request with a deadline and observes success, latency, a bounded degraded response, or an explicit failure.

nodes.label: DNS and edge
nodes.detail: Publishes the endpoint, terminates TLS, applies coarse protection, and steers traffic only to a region declared ready.

nodes.label: Regional balancer
nodes.detail: Routes requests across healthy zone endpoints. Platform owners define checks, draining, and the capacity required after a target is removed.

nodes.label: Service in zone A
nodes.detail: Runs stateless business logic with bounded calls. It can be replaced only if state, sessions, and deployment artifacts are outside the host.

nodes.label: Service in zone B
nodes.detail: Carries normal traffic and enough reserved capacity to accept work when the other zone is removed.

nodes.label: Authoritative database
nodes.detail: Owns acknowledged records, replication, failover fencing, backups, and proof that restored data satisfies application invariants.

nodes.label: Durable work queue
nodes.detail: Buffers accepted background work with explicit retention, redelivery, poison-message, lag, and overload policies.

nodes.label: Background worker
nodes.detail: Consumes durable work idempotently. A worker outage should increase queue age rather than erase accepted jobs or block unrelated requests.

nodes.label: Telemetry pipeline
nodes.detail: Collects metrics, logs, and traces and confirms its own freshness. Observability owners keep a separate signal for pipeline failure.

nodes.label: Recovery region
nodes.detail: Provides separately tested traffic entry, compute, data, secrets, and observability. It is usable only after failover authority and data state are verified.

scenarios.label: Healthy spread
scenarios.summary: Traffic is spread across two zones, acknowledged state goes to the database, deferred work enters the queue, and evidence leaves the response path asynchronously.
scenarios.result: Customers receive the normal response. Platform, application, data, and observability owners can each point to the signal and recovery action they own.

scenarios.label: Host loss
scenarios.summary: The zone A service endpoint fails its health check. The balancer removes it and surviving capacity in zone B carries the request path.
scenarios.result: The blast radius is one endpoint if health removal is fast and zone B has enough headroom. The platform owner replaces capacity while the application owner watches objective burn.

scenarios.label: Zone loss
scenarios.summary: Zone A disappears and the database runs in a degraded cross-zone state. All customer and background traffic now depends on zone B capacity.
scenarios.result: Customers stay online only if compute and data were provisioned and tested for the remaining zone. Freeze risky releases, restore redundancy, and verify backlog and replication health.

scenarios.label: Region loss
scenarios.summary: The primary regional entry, both service zones, database, and queue are unavailable. The edge can steer only after the recovery region is declared correct and ready.
scenarios.result: The blast radius is every primary-region user until failover completes. The incident commander verifies data authority and invokes the regional runbook; DNS or edge steering alone cannot make an untested stack recover.

scenarios.label: Telemetry loss
scenarios.summary: Customer traffic, durable writes, and background work continue, but metrics, logs, and traces are no longer arriving reliably.
scenarios.result: Immediate customer impact may be zero, but detection and diagnosis blast radius is broad. Stop promotion, use independent health evidence, restore the pipeline, and reconcile the missing interval.
